chunks: Ali ibn Muhammad, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Ammar ibn Marwan, who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), 'My father was near death, and he was told to make a will. He said, 'This is my son, meaning Umar; whatever he does is valid.' The Imam (peace be upon him) said, 'Your father has made a will and been concise.' I said, 'Indeed, he ordered for you such and such.' He said, 'Accept it.' I said, 'And he willed for a believing slave-girl. When we freed her, it became clear to us that she was not of sound judgment.' He said, 'It has sufficed for him.'
ai.seo_question: What is the validity of a father's will if he authorizes his son to decide the distribution or if he bequeaths a slave-girl who is not of sound judgment?
ai.summary: This narration from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the validity of testamentary bequests (wasiyyah) when the beneficiary's capacity is uncertain, establishing that the Imam's ratification ('ajzahu') validates the act even if the freed slave-girl is later found to be 'ghayr rashidah' (not fully of sound judgment). It highlights the Shia juristic principle that the testator's intent and the Imam's approval can supersede strict conditions of the beneficiary's maturity, ensuring the bequest remains legally binding. This underscores the flexibility in Shia inheritance law regarding the status of slaves and the authority of the Imam in validating estate distributions.
